clue.text: Numbers game

explanation.surface: A two-word note on the numbers game, as if about gambling or statistics.
explanation.definitionFit: Fives are several instances of the number five, and fives is also a British handball-style court game played at schools such as Eton.

clue.text: Anatole admitting his privilege

indicators.note: admitting means letting the following word inside the writer's surname

parts.note: Anatole France was the French novelist and Nobel laureate
taken as written

explanation.surface: The French author Anatole allowing in his own special right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitting' puts HIS inside FRANCE, between FRANC and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A franchise is a right or privilege granted, such as the right to vote.

clue.text: Old man about 100, a peer of Dr. Primrose

indicators.note: about here means going round, so the Latin word holds the other letters

parts.note: vir is the Latin, so old, word for a man
C is the Roman numeral for 100
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old man of about a hundred, contemporary of a certain doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Primrose is the clergyman narrator of Goldsmith's The Vicar of Wakefield, so his peer is another of his calling. 'about' puts CA inside VIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Primrose is a parish priest of the Church of England, so an equal of his holds the same clerical office.

clue.text: In what poet does Sir Patrick meet King Edward?

parts.note: Sir Patrick Spens is the hero of a famous Scottish ballad
ER stands for Edwardus Rex, King Edward

explanation.surface: Asking in which poet's work a ballad hero meets an English king.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmund Spenser was the Elizabethan author of The Faerie Queene.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Spenser was an English poet of the 16th century.

clue.text: Right to give directors leading roles

parts.note: to give someone leading roles is to star them in a production
a company's directors together form its board

explanation.surface: A claim that one is entitled to cast the company directors in the lead parts.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship the starboard side is the right-hand side when facing forward.

clue.text: Concluding she gives him my dance

indicators.note: concluding points to the closing letter of gives, which with the words after it runs on to spell the dance

explanation.surface: At the end she gives him her dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside 'gives him my', from the S that concludes 'gives'; the surface makes 'she gives him my dance' look like a ballroom favour.
explanation.definitionFit: The shimmy is a 1920s jazz dance in which the body shakes.

clue.text: Rita's unorthodox: attempt shows skill

indicators.note: unorthodox means not in the usual order, so Rita's letters are rearranged

parts.note: the name with its possessive s supplies five letters
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: Rita's unconventional attempt reveals her talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unorthodox' rearranges RITAS to ARTIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Artistry is creative skill or craft.

clue.text: What a blessing Jonson is being, staged

parts.note: Ben Jonson was the Jacobean playwright
taken as written
a play being staged is on

explanation.surface: Delight that a play by Jonson is being put on.
explanation.definitionFit: A benison is an old word for a blessing or benediction.

clue.text: Disney's liveliness

explanation.surface: A note on the energy of Walt Disney's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Disney's films are cartoons, made by drawing frames to move; and liveliness is vitality or spirit, the other sense.

clue.text: Many study with great apprehension

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number, so many
to read a subject is to study it

explanation.surface: Many people study in a state of anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' giving D relies on the crossword convention that any large Roman numeral can stand for many.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread is a great fear or anxious anticipation.

clue.text: Subtle as St. Michael, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the saint's name may be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A remark that a saint might be called subtle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subtle' looks like an adjective but is a proper name: Subtle is the con-man title character of Ben Jonson's comedy The Alchemist. 'possibly' rearranges ST MICHAEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Subtle is the fraudulent gold-making trickster who plays the title role in Jonson's 1610 play.

clue.text: Sound of a ' North European river

parts.note: the Oise is a river in northern France, a tributary of the Seine

explanation.surface: A question about the noise a river in northern Europe makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A noise is any sound, especially a loud or unwanted one.

clue.text: Present-day discovery in the — Indian (or Pacific) Ocean

definitions.text: Present-day discovery in the — Indian (or Pacific) Ocean

parts.words: Present-day discovery in the — Indian (or Pacific) Ocean
parts.note: present-day reads as the day of presents, 25 December: an island sighted and named on that day, with one such in the Indian Ocean and another in the Pacific

explanation.surface: A news item about a modern find somewhere in the Indian or Pacific Ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present-day' seems to mean modern; it means the day presents are given. The Indian Ocean island was named by a captain who passed it on 25 December 1643, and Cook named the Pacific one (Kiritimati) the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Both islands so called were named for the festive date on which European sailors first sighted them.

clue.text: Fashionable business, though ' failing

parts.note: something fashionable is said to be in
a firm is a business company

explanation.surface: A fashionable company that is nonetheless going under.
explanation.definitionFit: Failing in health or strength means weak and frail, the sense of infirm.

clue.text: Sources of sin at UN Assembly

indicators.note: assembly means putting the letters together into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Origins of wrongdoing at the United Nations General Assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assembly' looks like the UN body; it rearranges OF SIN AT UN.
explanation.definitionFit: A fountain is a source or spring, as in a fountain of knowledge.

clue.text: What Dobbin needs, of course, to flourish?

parts.note: Dobbin is a traditional name for a farm horse, and horses are fed bran
a dish is a course of a meal

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about what an old horse needs to thrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flourish' seems to mean thrive, as a well-fed horse would; it is the verb meaning wave about showily.
explanation.definitionFit: To flourish a sword or stick is to wave it about ostentatiously, the same action as brandishing it.

clue.text: East End pressman not employed originally

parts.note: Hackney is a borough in London's East End
ED is short for editor, a newspaper man

explanation.surface: A Cockney journalist who was out of work at first.
explanation.walkthrough: Hackney is a district of east London, the working-class East End.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackneyed means overused and trite, so phrases so described are never used in a fresh or original way.

clue.text: Part of stable — on entering one, find this?

definitions.text: Part of stable — on entering one, find this?

parts.note: a stall is a compartment in a stable
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Going into one of a stable's compartments and expecting a particular animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entering' just places ON after I. The whole clue also describes the answer: a male horse is what you find in a stall.
explanation.definitionFit: A stallion is an uncastrated male horse, kept in a stable stall.

clue.text: Condition of peers requiring casting vote

definitions.text: Condition of peers requiring casting vote

parts.words: Condition of peers requiring casting vote
parts.note: peers read as equals rather than lords, and a tied vote between equal sides is settled by the chair's casting vote

explanation.surface: A remark about the House of Lords needing a deciding vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peers' suggests members of the House of Lords; it means people who are level with each other, as in a tied ballot.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on a par with one another is the state of sameness in status, and a tie in votes is that state.

clue.text: Support for the Scriptures

parts.note: support reads as backing for religious belief, but is a physical stand on which the Bible rests in church

explanation.surface: A phrase about backing for religious belief.
explanation.definitionFit: In church the Bible is read from a sloping reading desk, which literally holds it up.

clue.text: Can the commander return for a drink?

indicators.note: return asks for the joined words to be turned round and read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
GOC is the military abbreviation for General Officer Commanding

explanation.surface: Asking whether the commanding officer can come back for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reverses CANGOC as a whole to give the brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognac is a brandy from the Cognac region of France, a spirit drunk after dinner.

clue.text: Pupils' examiner

parts.note: pupils read as schoolchildren, an examiner who tests them, but here they are the openings in the eyes

explanation.surface: Someone who sets exams for schoolchildren.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye doctor looks into the eyes and so examines the dark centres of the irises.

clue.text: The province of a student's champion

parts.note: L, the learner plate letter, stands for a student, plus the possessive s
an ace is a champion or expert

explanation.surface: Asking which region a student's hero belongs to.
explanation.walkthrough: L-plates mark a learner driver in Britain, so L is a student.
explanation.definitionFit: Alsace is a historic region of north-east France on the Rhine.

clue.text: A sight better if this error were avoided

definitions.text: A sight better if this error were avoided

parts.words: A sight better if this error were avoided
parts.note: a sight is both a great deal and literally something seen; a mistake of vision makes things look other than they are

explanation.surface: A remark that things would be a great deal better without a certain mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sight better' reads as the idiom 'much better'; literally, eyesight would be better without a trick of the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A trick of perception in which the eye is deceived into seeing what is not there is an error of sight.

clue.text: Aquatic carnivore closer to what 'e's 'unting

indicators.note: dropped aitches mark Cockney speech, so the word loses its H

parts.note: in a hunting game, getting closer is getting hotter

explanation.surface: A Cockney huntsman nearing the animal he is chasing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what 'e's 'unting' drops H as in Cockney speech, so HOTTER loses its H; otter-hunting was once a field sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The otter is a fish-eating mammal that lives in rivers.

clue.text: Senseless girl that's outside

indicators.note: outside means the abbreviation goes round the name

parts.note: i.e. is the Latin abbreviation id est, that is
Nan is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A foolish girl who has been left outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's outside' looks like a description of the girl; 'that's' gives IE and 'outside' wraps it round NAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means silly or lacking sense.

clue.text: Journey east for a Lancastrian dish

parts.note: a trip is a journey

explanation.surface: Travelling east to sample a Lancashire speciality.
explanation.walkthrough: A Lancastrian comes from Lancashire, a county in north-west England where cow's stomach lining with onions is a traditional food.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe, the stomach lining of cattle, is a dish strongly associated with Lancashire cooking.

clue.text: One girl swallowing a drink? Fancy

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: swallowing means the girl's name takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: Mary is a girl's name
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: A girl downing a drink, followed by a question of whether this is just a fancy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallowing' puts A GIN inside MARY after its M, giving MAGINARY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fancied rather than real exists only in the mind, which is what imaginary means.

clue.text: Echo, effect once associated with Arne's composition

indicators.note: composition hints at music but signals the letters being put together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Thomas Arne was the 18th-century English composer of Rule, Britannia

explanation.surface: A musical echo effect once heard in a piece by the composer Arne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' rearranges ONCE plus ARNES.
explanation.definitionFit: Resonance is the prolonging of a sound by reflection or vibration, an echoing effect.

clue.text: River for Harris, and others

explanation.surface: Naming a river suitable for a man called Harris and his friends.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tweed is a river on the Scottish border, and Harris is a famous hand-woven woollen cloth of that kind from the Outer Hebrides.
